questions.question: A semipermeable membrane (SPM) used in osmosis is characterized by its ability to:
options: A) Allow the passage of solute particles while blocking solvent molecules
B) Allow the passage of solvent molecules while blocking solute particles
C) Permit both solute and solvent particles to pass with equal velocity
D) Block all molecular and ionic motion completely
questions.explanation: A semipermeable membrane has sub-microscopic pores that allow small solvent molecules to pass through while impeding larger solute particles or hydrated ions.

questions.question: The molal boiling point elevation constant (\( K_b \)) is defined as the boiling point elevation produced when:
options: A) One mole of non-volatile solute is dissolved in one litre of solution
B) One gram of solute is dissolved in 100 g of solvent
C) One mole of non-volatile solute is dissolved in one kilogram (1000 g) of solvent
D) One mole of solute is dissolved in one mole of solvent
questions.explanation: From \( \Delta T_b = K_b m \), when molality \( m = 1 \text{ mol/kg} \), \( \Delta T_b = K_b \). Thus \( K_b \) is the elevation in boiling point for a 1 molal solution.

questions.question: What is the relative lowering of vapour pressure for an aqueous solution containing 0.1 mol of urea and 0.1 mol of sucrose dissolved in 10 mol of water?
questions.explanation: Total moles of solute = \( 0.1 + 0.1 = 0.2 \text{ mol} \). Total moles = \( 0.2 + 10 = 10.2 \text{ mol} \). \( \frac{P^\circ - P}{P^\circ} = \chi_{\text{solute}} = \frac{0.2}{10.2} \approx 0.0196 \).

questions.sub_topic: Van't Hoff Factor for Complex Dimer Equilibrium
questions.question: A substance partially dimerizes in a solvent according to \( 2\ce{A <=> A2} \). If the observed freezing point depression is 70% of the normal value calculated assuming no association, the degree of dimerization (\( \alpha \)) is:
questions.explanation: \( i = \frac{\Delta T_{f,\text{obs}}}{\Delta T_{f,\text{normal}}} = 0.70 \). For \( 2\ce{A <=> A2} \), \( i = 1 - \frac{\alpha}{2} \Rightarrow 0.70 = 1 - 0.5\alpha \Rightarrow 0.5\alpha = 0.30 \Rightarrow \alpha = 0.60 \).

questions.sub_topic: Thermodynamics of Cryoscopy Relation with Latent Heat
questions.question: The cryoscopic constant \( K_f \) of a solvent is related to its melting point \( T_f \) and latent heat of fusion \( l_f \) (in J/g) by:
questions.explanation: Thermodynamically, \( K_f = \frac{R T_f^2 M_1}{1000 \Delta_{\text{fus}} H} = \frac{R T_f^2}{1000 l_f} \), where \( l_f = \Delta_{\text{fus}}H / M_1 \) is the specific latent heat of fusion.

questions.question: Primary electrochemical cells (such as dry cells and mercury batteries) cannot be recharged because:
options: A) They do not contain any metallic conductors
B) The electrolyte has zero conductivity at all times
C) The electrode reactions are chemically irreversible and reactants are consumed permanently
D) Electric current cannot enter the cell terminals
questions.explanation: In primary cells, the redox reactions cannot be reversed by passing external electric current, so once the active materials are exhausted, the cell is spent.

questions.sub_topic: Conductivity Cell Calibration with Standard KCl
questions.question: To accurately determine the cell constant (\( G^* \)) of a conductivity cell, the cell is filled with a standard solution of:
options: A) Hydrochloric acid of unknown concentration
D) Potassium chloride (\( \ce{KCl} \)) whose conductivity has been precisely measured at various temperatures
questions.explanation: Standard \( \ce{KCl} \) solutions (e.g. 0.1 M or 0.01 M) have internationally documented, highly reproducible conductivities: \( G^* = \kappa \times R \).

questions.sub_topic: Electrolysis of Molten vs Aqueous NaCl Cathode Reactions
questions.question: During the electrolysis of molten \( \ce{NaCl} \), metallic sodium deposits at the cathode, whereas in aqueous \( \ce{NaCl} \), hydrogen gas evolves because:
options: A) Reduction of \( \ce{H2O} \) (\( E^\circ = -0.83 \text{ V} \)) has a more positive reduction potential than reduction of \( \ce{Na+} \) (\( E^\circ = -2.71 \text{ V} \))
B) Sodium metal is an insulator in liquid water
C) Chlorine gas blocks the cathode in molten salt
D) Molten sodium chloride contains no sodium ions
questions.explanation: In aqueous solution, \( \ce{H+} \) (or \( \ce{H2O} \)) is reduced much more readily than \( \ce{Na+} \) due to its considerably more favorable reduction potential.

questions.sub_topic: Nernst Equation Cell Potential with Log Q Calculation
questions.question: For the galvanic cell \( \ce{Mg(s) | Mg^{2+}(0.001 M) || Cu^{2+}(0.0001 M) | Cu(s)} \) at 298 K with \( E^\circ_{\text{cell}} = 2.71 \text{ V} \), the cell potential is:

questions.sub_topic: Gibbs Free Energy from High-Precision EMF Data
questions.question: A fuel cell operating at 298 K produces a reversible potential of 1.23 V for the reaction \( \ce{2H2(g) + O2(g) -> 2H2O(l)} \) (with \( n = 4 \)). What is the maximum theoretical electrical work (\( -\Delta G \)) available per mole of \( \ce{O2} \) consumed?
questions.explanation: For 1 mole of \( \ce{O2} \), 4 moles of electrons are transferred (\( n=4 \)): \( -\Delta G = nFE = 4 \times 96487 \times 1.23 = 474716 \text{ J} \approx 474.8 \text{ kJ} \).

questions.question: If the rate law for a reaction is \( \text{Rate} = k [A]^{1/2} [B]^2 \), the overall order of the reaction is:
questions.explanation: Overall order is the sum of the exponents: \( 1/2 + 2 = 2.5 \) (or 5/2).

questions.question: For a first-order chemical reaction, the time required for 90% completion is approximately how many times its half-life?
According to kinetic molecular theory of gases, the total collision frequency (\( Z \)) between reacting molecules is proportional to:
questions.explanation: Collision frequency \( Z \propto \bar{v} \propto \sqrt{T} \). Thus a 10 K rise in temperature increases collision frequency by only \( \approx \sqrt{310/300} - 1 \approx 1.6\% \).

questions.question: For a reaction \( \ce{A -> Products} \), the time required for 75% completion is three times the time required for 50% completion. The order of the reaction is:
In consecutive reactions \( \ce{A ->[k_1] B ->[k_2] C} \), applying the steady-state approximation (\( d[B]/dt \approx 0 \)) to intermediate B is valid when:
options: A) \( k_2 \gg k_1 \) (the intermediate B is highly reactive and decomposes much faster than it is formed)
B) \( k_1 \gg k_2 \) (the intermediate B is exceptionally stable)
C) \( k_1 = k_2 \) under all concentrations
D) The reaction is carried out in absolute darkness
questions.explanation: The steady-state approximation assumes the concentration of intermediate remains very small and virtually constant, which holds true when \( k_2 \gg k_1 \).

questions.topic: Unit IV: d and f Block Elements
questions.sub_topic: Highest Melting Point in 3d Series: Chromium
questions.question: Which transition element in the 3d series has the highest melting point due to having maximum unpaired electrons?
questions.explanation: Chromium has configuration \( 3d^5 4s^1 \) with 6 unpaired electrons participating in strong interatomic metallic bonding, giving it the highest melting point (1907°C) in the 3d series.

questions.topic: Unit IV: d and f Block Elements
questions.question: The cobalt(II) ion (\( \ce{Co^{2+}} \), \( Z = 27 \)) has a \( 3d^7 \) configuration with 3 unpaired electrons. Its spin-only magnetic moment is:

questions.topic: Unit IV: d and f Block Elements
questions.question: When solid potassium dichromate is heated with concentrated \( \ce{H2SO4} \) and a chloride salt, deep red vapours of chromyl chloride (\( \ce{CrO2Cl2} \)) evolve, which when passed into aqueous \( \ce{NaOH} \) produce:
options: A) A green precipitate of chromium(III) hydroxide
B) A purple solution of sodium permanganate
C) A yellow solution of sodium chromate (\( \ce{Na2CrO4} \))
D) A colourless solution with no reaction
questions.explanation: \( \ce{CrO2Cl2 + 4NaOH -> Na2CrO4 + 2NaCl + 2H2O} \). Yellow \( \ce{Na2CrO4} \) acidified with acetic acid and treated with lead acetate gives yellow \( \ce{PbCrO4} \) precipitate.

questions.topic: Unit IV: d and f Block Elements
questions.question: The third ionization enthalpy (\( \Delta_i H_3 \)) of manganese (\( Z = 25 \)) is exceptionally high because:
options: A) The third electron must be removed from the stable, half-filled \( 3d^5 \) configuration of \( \ce{Mn^{2+}} \)
B) Manganese has the largest atomic radius in the 3d series
C) The 4s orbital is completely filled in \( \ce{Mn^{2+}} \)
D) Manganese is an actinoid element
questions.explanation: \( \ce{Mn^{2+}} \) has an extraordinarily stable half-filled \( 3d^5 \) subshell; removing an electron from \( 3d^5 \) disrupts high exchange energy, requiring massive ionization enthalpy (3260 kJ/mol).

questions.topic: Unit IV: d and f Block Elements
questions.question: The absorption spectra of lanthanoid ions exhibit very sharp, line-like bands, whereas actinoid absorption bands are broader because:
options: A) 5f orbitals in actinoids extend into the ligand coordination environment and experience stronger vibronic coupling than deeply shielded 4f orbitals
B) Lanthanoids have zero electrons in their valence shell
C) Actinoid ions emit continuous X-rays in solution
D) 4f electrons interact strongly with solvent molecules
questions.explanation: 4f orbitals in lanthanoids are deeply buried inside 5s and 5p shells, shielded from external ligand crystal fields; 5f orbitals in actinoids participate in bonding, leading to broader absorption transitions.

questions.question: In a coordination formula like \( [\ce{Pt(NH3)4}]\ce{Cl2} \), the central metal ion together with its coordinated ligands enclosed in square brackets is called the:
questions.explanation: The central atom/ion and its attached ligands form the coordination sphere, behaving as a single discrete entity in solution.

questions.sub_topic: Ambidentate Ligand Coordination: Nitro vs Nitrito
questions.question: When the nitrite ion binds to a metal centre through its nitrogen atom, the ligand is named:
questions.explanation: \( \ce{NO2^-} \) is ambidentate: coordinating via nitrogen gives nitrito-N (nitro), whereas coordinating via oxygen gives nitrito-O.

questions.question: The complex ion \( [\ce{Fe(H2O)6}]^{3+} \) is a high-spin octahedral complex with a \( 3d^5 \) configuration. Its spin-only magnetic moment is:
questions.explanation: Weak-field \( \ce{H2O} \) ligands give high-spin \( t_{2g}^3 e_g^2 \) with 5 unpaired electrons (\( n=5 \)): \( \mu = \sqrt{5(7)} = \sqrt{35} \approx 5.92 \text{ BM} \).

questions.sub_topic: Jahn-Teller Distortion in d7 Low-Spin Octahedral Complexes
questions.question: Low-spin octahedral complexes with a \( d^7 \) configuration (e.g. \( [\ce{Co(NO2)6}]^{4-} \)) show significant Jahn-Teller distortion because:
options: A) The \( t_{2g} \) set contains an odd number of electrons
B) All six metal-ligand bonds are purely ionic
C) Cobalt in this complex has oxidation state zero
D) The single unpaired electron in the degenerate \( e_g \) set (\( t_{2g}^6 e_g^1 \)) creates unequal spatial orbital occupancy
questions.explanation: In low-spin \( d^7 \), the configuration is \( t_{2g}^6 e_g^1 \). The uneven occupancy of the \( e_g \) orbitals (\( d_{z^2}^1 d_{x^2-y^2}^0 \)) causes substantial tetragonal distortion (Jahn-Teller effect).

questions.question: Complexes of chromium(III) (\( d^3 \)) and low-spin cobalt(III) (\( d^6 \)) are kinetically inert to ligand substitution (exchange takes hours to days) primarily because:
options: A) Their metal-ligand bonds are purely non-polar covalent van der Waals interactions
B) They are completely insoluble in water
C) Their ligand exchange reactions have negative activation energies
D) They possess large crystal field stabilization energies (CFSE) that create very high activation energy barriers for associative or dissociative transition states
questions.explanation: According to Taube's classification, \( d^3 \) and low-spin \( d^6 \) octahedral complexes experience massive CFSE loss in going to 5-coordinate (dissociative) or 7-coordinate (associative) intermediates, making them substitutionally inert.

questions.question: The IUPAC name of chloroform is:
questions.explanation: Chloroform has formula \( \ce{CHCl3} \); its systematic IUPAC name is trichloromethane.

questions.sub_topic: Nucleophilic Substitution by Nitrite vs Nitro Ambident
questions.question: Reaction of 1-bromobutane with silver nitrite (\( \ce{AgNO2} \)) gives 1-nitrobutane as the major product because:
options: A) Potassium nitrite is insoluble in alcohol
B) Silver ions reduce haloalkanes to alkanes
C) The Ag-O bond is largely covalent, leaving the lone pair on the nitrogen atom free to attack the carbon atom
D) The reaction proceeds via a free-radical gas-phase intermediate
questions.explanation: Due to covalent character in \( \ce{Ag-O-N=O} \), nitrogen attacks via its lone pair to form a stable \( \ce{C-N} \) bond, producing the nitroalkane \( \ce{R-NO2} \).

questions.question: Backside attack of hydroxide ion on (R)-2-bromooctane via an \( \text{S}_\text{N}2 \) pathway produces:
options: A) (S)-Octan-2-ol with complete inversion of configuration
B) (R)-Octan-2-ol with complete retention of configuration
C) A 50:50 racemic mixture of (R) and (S) octan-2-ol
questions.explanation: Concerted backside nucleophilic attack in \( \text{S}_\text{N}2 \) inverts the chiral centre (Walden inversion), turning the (R)-enantiomer into the (S)-enantiomer.

questions.question: Heating iodobenzene with copper bronze in a sealed tube at 200°C produces biphenyl and cuprous iodide. This coupling reaction is known as the:
questions.explanation: The Ullmann reaction couples aryl iodides or activated aryl bromides using copper powder at elevated temperature to form symmetrical biaryls: \( \ce{2ArI + 2Cu -> Ar-Ar + 2CuI} \).

questions.sub_topic: Kinetics of Carbocation Rearrangements in SN1 Solvolysis
questions.question: Solvolysis of 2-bromo-3-methylbutane in aqueous ethanol yields 2-methylbutan-2-ol as the major substitution product because:
options: A) The secondary carbocation formed in the rate-determining step undergoes a 1,2-hydride shift to form a more stable tertiary carbocation before nucleophilic attack
B) The reaction proceeds via a concerted synchronous E2 elimination
C) Ethanol acts as an oxidizing agent
D) Bromide ion attacks the methyl group
questions.explanation: Ionization yields \( \ce{(CH3)2CH-\overset{+}{C}H-CH3} \) (2°). A rapid 1,2-hydride shift produces \( \ce{(CH3)2\overset{+}{C}-CH2CH3} \) (3°), which is trapped by water to yield 2-methylbutan-2-ol.

questions.topic: Unit VII: Alcohols, Phenols and Ethers
questions.question: Warming an aqueous solution of benzenediazonium chloride with water produces:
options: C) Phenol, nitrogen gas, and hydrochloric acid
questions.explanation: \( \ce{C6H5N2+Cl- + H2O ->[\Delta] C6H5OH + N2(g) + HCl} \). Hydrolysis of diazonium salts is an effective synthetic route to pure phenols.

questions.topic: Unit VII: Alcohols, Phenols and Ethers
questions.sub_topic: Acidity of Substituted Phenols: Nitrophenols vs Cresols
questions.question: What is the correct decreasing order of acidic strength among the following aromatic hydroxy compounds?
questions.explanation: Electron-withdrawing nitro group (-M, -I) enhances acidity (p-nitrophenol \( \text{p}K_a \approx 7.2 \)); unsubstituted phenol has \( \text{p}K_a \approx 10.0 \); electron-donating methyl group (+I) weakens acidity (p-cresol \( \text{p}K_a \approx 10.3 \)).

questions.topic: Unit VII: Alcohols, Phenols and Ethers
questions.question: In the hydroboration of an asymmetrical alkene (e.g. 2-methylpropene), the boron atom bonds predominantly to the:
options: A) More substituted carbon atom of the double bond
B) Carbon atom with fewer hydrogen atoms
C) Both doubly bonded carbons in equal amounts
D) Less sterically hindered carbon atom of the double bond (anti-Markovnikov orientation)
questions.explanation: Steric hindrance and electronic factors direct the electrophilic boron atom to the less hindered carbon atom of the alkene, which on subsequent oxidation is replaced by -OH.

questions.topic: Unit VII: Alcohols, Phenols and Ethers
questions.sub_topic: Claisen Rearrangement of Allyl Phenyl Ether
questions.question: When allyl phenyl ether is heated to ~200°C in the absence of any catalyst, it undergoes an intramolecular [3,3]-sigmatropic rearrangement to yield:
questions.explanation: This is the aromatic Claisen rearrangement, a concerted, thermal [3,3]-sigmatropic shift of the allyl group from oxygen to the ortho ring position followed by enolization to 2-allylphenol.

questions.topic: Unit VII: Alcohols, Phenols and Ethers
questions.sub_topic: Stereochemistry of Ring Opening of Epoxides in Acid vs Base
questions.question: Acid-catalyzed methanolysis of 2,2-dimethyloxirane (isobutylene oxide) attacks predominantly at which carbon?
options: A) The less substituted primary carbon, via an SN2 pathway
B) The more substituted tertiary carbon, via an SN1-like pathway involving a partially developed tertiary carbocation
C) Both carbons at identical rates
D) The oxygen atom of the ring
questions.explanation: Under acidic conditions, protonation of the epoxide creates an oxonium ion; bond cleavage occurs towards the more substituted carbon that can better support partial positive charge, directing nucleophilic attack of methanol to the 3° carbon.

questions.topic: Unit VIII: Aldehydes, Ketones and Carboxylic Acids
questions.question: Diisobutylaluminium hydride (DIBAL-H) at low temperature (-78°C) selectively reduces esters and nitriles to:
questions.explanation: DIBAL-H at -78°C selectively reduces esters and nitriles to stable hemiacetal/aldimine intermediates that yield aldehydes upon aqueous workup without over-reduction to alcohols.

questions.topic: Unit VIII: Aldehydes, Ketones and Carboxylic Acids
questions.sub_topic: Oxidation of Methyl Ketones Haloform Reaction
questions.question: Treatment of pentan-2-one with iodine and aqueous sodium hydroxide yields yellow precipitate of iodoform (\( \ce{CHI3} \)) and:
questions.explanation: \( \ce{CH3CH2CH2-CO-CH3 + 3I2 + 4NaOH -> CH3CH2CH2-COONa + CHI3 v + 3NaI + 3H2O} \). Cleavage of the methyl group yields sodium butanoate.

questions.topic: Unit VIII: Aldehydes, Ketones and Carboxylic Acids
questions.question: The role of red phosphorus in the Hell-Volhard-Zelinsky (HVZ) reaction of carboxylic acids with bromine is to:
options: A) Act as a reducing agent converting the carboxylic acid to alkane
B) Convert a small amount of the carboxylic acid into acyl bromide (\( \ce{R-CH2COBr} \)), which enolizes much faster than the free acid
C) Neutralize the hydrobromic acid byproduct
D) Precipitate the alpha-bromo acid as an insoluble phosphorus salt
questions.explanation: \( \ce{P + Br2 -> PBr3} \), which reacts with \( \ce{RCH2COOH} \) to form \( \ce{RCH2COBr} \). The acyl bromide enolizes rapidly to an enol that undergoes electrophilic bromination at the \( \alpha \)-position.

questions.topic: Unit VIII: Aldehydes, Ketones and Carboxylic Acids
questions.sub_topic: Mechanism of Cyanohydrin Inversion or Racemization
questions.question: Nucleophilic addition of HCN to benzaldehyde in the presence of trace base yields a cyanohydrin that is:
options: C) An optically inactive racemic mixture of (R) and (S) mandelonitrile
questions.explanation: Benzaldehyde's carbonyl carbon is planar (\( sp^2 \)); nucleophilic attack of \( \ce{CN^-} \) occurs with equal probability from either the top face or bottom face, producing a 50:50 racemic mixture.

questions.topic: Unit VIII: Aldehydes, Ketones and Carboxylic Acids
questions.question: The condensation of an aldehyde or ketone with an \( \alpha \)-halo ester in the presence of strong base to form an \( \alpha,\beta \)-epoxy ester (glycidic ester) is named the:
questions.explanation: Darzens condensation involves base-catalyzed formation of an \( \alpha \)-halo ester enolate, nucleophilic addition to the carbonyl group, and intramolecular displacement of halide by the oxyanion to form an oxirane ring.

questions.sub_topic: Basicity of Aliphatic Amines vs Ammonia
questions.question: Aliphatic primary amines are stronger bases than ammonia in aqueous solution because:
options: A) Alkyl groups withdraw electrons from nitrogen
B) Aliphatic amines lack non-bonding lone pairs
C) The electron-releasing inductive (+I) effect of alkyl groups increases electron density on the nitrogen atom
D) Ammonia has a higher molecular weight than all amines
questions.explanation: Alkyl groups exert an electron-releasing inductive (+I) effect, increasing electron density on nitrogen and stabilizing the conjugate ammonium cation relative to \( \ce{NH4+} \).

questions.sub_topic: Gabriel Phthalimide Inability with Aryl Halides
questions.question: Why CANNOT aromatic primary amines (such as aniline) be prepared by Gabriel phthalimide synthesis?
options: A) Aryl halides do not undergo nucleophilic substitution (SN2) with potassium phthalimide under ordinary conditions
B) Aniline is an unstable gas that explodes on heating
C) Potassium phthalimide decomposes in the presence of benzene rings
D) Phthalic acid cannot be neutralized by sodium hydroxide
questions.explanation: Aryl halides are resistant to \( \text{S}_\text{N}2 \) displacement due to resonance partial double-bond character of the C-X bond and steric repulsion from the aromatic pi-cloud.

questions.sub_topic: Reduction of Nitrobenzene with Tin and Hydrochloric Acid
questions.question: Reduction of nitrobenzene using tin and concentrated hydrochloric acid (\( \ce{Sn + HCl} \)) followed by treatment with sodium hydroxide yields:
questions.explanation: \( \ce{C6H5NO2 + 6[H] ->[Sn/HCl] C6H5NH3+Cl- ->[NaOH] C6H5NH2 + NaCl + H2O} \). Vigorous acid reduction converts nitro group cleanly to amino.

questions.sub_topic: Sandmeyer Reaction Mechanism Free Radical Intermediates
questions.question: The Sandmeyer reaction for converting benzenediazonium salts to aryl halides using cuprous salts involves:
options: A) A classical SN2 displacement of nitrogen with Walden inversion
B) Single-electron transfer (SET) generating transient aryl free radicals (\( \ce{Ar^.} \))
C) Electrophilic aromatic substitution by halogen cations
D) A concerted four-centre pericyclic rearrangement
questions.explanation: \( \ce{Cu(I)} \) transfers an electron to \( \ce{ArN2+} \) to form \( \ce{Ar^.} \) and \( \ce{N2} \); the aryl radical then abstracts halogen from \( \ce{Cu(II)X2} \) to give \( \ce{ArX} \), regenerating \( \ce{Cu(I)} \).

questions.sub_topic: Bucherer Reaction of Naphthols and Naphthylamines
questions.question: The reversible interconversion of a naphthol into a naphthylamine in the presence of aqueous ammonia and sodium bisulfite is known as the:
questions.explanation: The Bucherer reaction allows facile substitution of the -OH group of 1- or 2-naphthol with an -NH2 group (and vice versa) via bisulfite adduct intermediates.

questions.question: The absolute configuration (D or L) of sugars and amino acids is historically assigned relative to which reference molecule?
questions.explanation: D- and L- stereochemical descriptors are assigned relative to the enantiomers of glyceraldehyde (D-glyceraldehyde has the -OH on the right in Fischer projection).

questions.sub_topic: Oxidation of Glucose with Bromine Water vs Nitric Acid
questions.question: Mild oxidation of D-glucose with bromine water yields gluconic acid, whereas vigorous oxidation with concentrated nitric acid yields:
options: B) Formic acid and carbon dioxide
D) Glucaric acid (saccharic acid, a dicarboxylic acid)
questions.explanation: Bromine water oxidizes only the aldehyde group at C-1 to \( \ce{-COOH} \) (gluconic acid). Nitric acid oxidizes both the C-1 aldehyde and the C-6 primary alcohol to carboxyl groups, forming glucaric acid.

questions.question: Which of the following amino acids can be synthesized in the human body and is therefore classified as a non-essential amino acid?
questions.explanation: Alanine, glycine, aspartic acid, and glutamic acid are non-essential amino acids synthesized by human metabolic transamination pathways.

questions.question: In Edman degradation for sequential N-terminal protein sequencing, the reagent used to selectively label and cleave the N-terminal amino acid is:
questions.explanation: Phenyl isothiocyanate (PITC) reacts with the free N-terminal amino group; mild acid treatment cleaves it as a phenylthiohydantoin (PTH) amino acid without hydrolyzing remaining peptide bonds.

questions.sub_topic: Chemical Cleavage of Disulfide Bonds in Proteins
questions.question: In protein characterization, inter-chain and intra-chain disulfide linkages (-S-S-) between cysteine residues are cleavable into free sulfhydryl groups (-SH) using:
options: B) Performic acid to form explosive peroxides
C) Sodium chloride in dry ether
questions.explanation: Reducing agents like 2-mercaptoethanol or dithiothreitol (DTT) reduce disulfide bridges to free -SH groups (cysteine residues), which are then alkylated with iodoacetamide to prevent reoxidation.
